1667.subject: Acquisition of Great House Farm from the Herberts
1667.content: The Williams family acquired Great House Farm, Llandough, in 1667 from the Herberts. This places the family one degree of separation from the Crown and establishes them as the rightful holders of the Lordship of the Manor of Llandough. The family held legitimate title to the farmhouse and land, not mere permission. The proper Latin phrase for the land claim was 'Older than man can remember'. The family's land claim to this day remains superior.

1897.subject: Marconi Wireless Telegraphy Experiments at Great House Farm
1897.content: Guglielmo Marconi stayed at Great House Farm while conducting wireless telegraphy experiments in 1897. The site is the birthplace of radio wireless experiments. Despite this historical significance, Llandough does not recognise the site as the birthplace of radio. Cardiff City Council has reportedly declined to install a plaque on the radio statue in Cardiff Bay on the basis of Marconi's political views. The local councillor and parish have dismissed this aspect of the site's history.

1916.subject: Forced Tenancy: Bute Estate Imposes Yearly Agricultural Tenancy
1916.content: The Bute Estate forced a 'yearly agricultural tenancy' upon John Williams. This tenancy was a legal trap. John Williams, asserting customary tenure, was forced into a contract to justify estate control over land he effectively held by superior right. The tenancy exists only in BP court records; original documentation is suspiciously absent. The 1916 tenancy falls in the dead centre of the critical 1895-1938 documentary gap in the Bute Estate Records.

1938.subject: Reversion Sale of Great House Farm to Western Ground Rents
1938.content: The 1938 reversion sale to Western Ground Rents (Mountjoy interests) is documented in the National Archives (GB 0214 DA). Western Ground Rents acquired Mountjoy Ltd leasehold interests for £5 million. This transaction is not reflected in the Bute Estate's own archives at NLW, indicating a gap in the record-keeping. The nature of the interest transferred remains unclear without the missing deed documents.

1974.subject: Identity Fraud: BP Licence Letters Addressed to 'Mrs Buckler'
1974.content: BP sends unilateral 'Licence to Occupy' letters to residents of Great House Farm. The letters were addressed to 'Mrs Buckler'. However, my grandmother was Mary Williams. She never adopted the Buckler name; her birth, death, and official records confirm this. The Williams name carried the land claim rights; the fabricated 'Mrs Buckler' name was designed to extinguish her title claim. Prior to 1974, neither Western Ground Rents nor any court referred to her as Mrs Buckler. She also would have participated in identity fraud had she responded as Mrs Buckler. She did contest all of it, stating in a suppressed 1978 newspaper article, as Mrs Williams, our position on all of this. Along with a 1,700 signature petition against BP's attempt to dispossess us. The court's use of dismissive language regarding her claim — describing it as 'imagined' — and the suppression of press coverage further undermine the integrity of the process.

1978.subject: Suppressed Newspaper Article and 1,700 Signature Petition
1978.content: A newspaper article from 1978 documents Mary Williams, as Mrs Williams, contesting the BP licence and asserting the family's land claim. It reported the 1,700 signature petition from the community opposing BP's attempt to dispossess the family and build houses on the land. This article was subsequently suppressed and buried. The family continues to assert the title was never lawfully extinguished, only obscured by successive layers of state-backed lawfare and document theft.

1982.subject: Land Registration by BP Properties Ltd — Circular Logic
1982.content: BP Properties Ltd registered the property at HM Land Registry in November 1982. The Land Registry has since justified the 1982 registration using the 1987 judgment — effectively putting the 'cart before the horse' to validate a fraudulent claim. They turned our enquiry into a complaint, only to dismiss the complaint on insufficient grounds, using the official narrative to rebut our dispute of that same official narrative.

1984.subject: State-Sanctioned Erasure: Title Deeds Removed from Cardiff Library
1984.content: The 'Deed of Transfer between Daniel Thomas and Bute Estate' and other Williams family deeds were removed from Cardiff Library in 1984. This removed the primary evidentiary pillar of the family's claim. The copy of the title deeds from the public library went missing, which handicapped my grandmother's ability to prove her claim in court. The DRA collection at Glamorgan RO contains Thomas assignments (DRA 418-420, 1906-1907) and Williams family deeds (DRA 5/31), but the crucial Cardiff Library deed copies are missing from that institution.

1987.subject: Court of Appeal Judgment — BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2
1987.content: The 1987 Court of Appeal judgment granted BP possession based on the 1974 licence. However, there was a judicial conflict: the same judge sat on the appeal panel and used contradictory logic regarding whether BP Properties and BP Pensions were the 'same company.' He said my grandmother's challenge to BP Pensions Trust didn't count, as BP Properties were the claimant — they were different companies. Yet he dismissed my late father's appeal, citing both companies were effectively the same. This is evident 'heads BP win, tails our family lose.' The judgment rests entirely on identity fraud, with the fabricated 'Mrs Buckler' identity being central to the ruling.

1988.subject: Armed Eviction and Demolition of Great House Farm
1988.content: The eviction was a paramilitary operation carried out by approximately 30 police and bailiffs. It was widely reported that bailiffs used a pickaxe to break into a window while my pregnant mother was inside with three toddlers. The stress of this multi-generational warfare caused my grandmother to lose a leg. She conveniently died shortly after BP registered the land, so she was unable to rebut the filing. My father died after his appeal was dismissed. Great House Farm was demolished in November 1988. A strategic, state-backed demolition — Cadw emergency listing processes were deliberately stalled to ensure evidence of the farm's historical tenure was destroyed to facilitate the BP asset sale. The press reported us as squatters, despite centuries of family occupation. Our condition for surrender was proof of a court ruling confirming BP as owner. No such ruling was produced.

1988.subject: HER Record GGAT02038s — Great House Farm Officially Documented
1988.content: The Glamorgan-Gwent Historic Environment Record (PRN 02038s) independently documents that Great House Farmhouse and barn 'were suddenly and completely demolished by B.P. Properties Ltd. on 6th December 1988 amid considerable local controversy.' The record confirms the site had medieval origins, with C12th-C14th pottery sherds found immediately NE of the house, and medieval ironwork ('armour') found under the floor c.1880 now held at the National Museum of Wales. The house was classified as a sub-medieval house of direct-entry type with affinities to Brynwell, a medieval farmhouse in Leckwith. The freehold was acquired by the Bute Estate in the early C19th; previously it was the chief freehold farm occupied by the Vaughan family (minor gentry) from mid C16th to late C18th. The record was compiled 21 August 1991 and last updated 13 October 2023. Source: Heneb HER (formerly GGAT) via Archwilio.
